name: 166. Session key affinity on an OpenAI-backed custom provider (session-key-affinity)
description:
Wire-level pins for the key half of session affinity. Folders 115 and 116 pin which provider a session follows, but every request there runs on a key a routing rule pins or on a pool a virtual key cuts to one key, so a session never answers with a key of its own in them.

Each row stands up its own run-scoped custom provider on the OpenAI base with keys that share one real credential, so only key selection decides which key serves, and uses key weights to make the outcome deterministic: a weight-0 key is never picked by ordinary selection beside a weighted one, so a request served on it got there through the session. Every row ends with a control request that shows the weights alone pick a different key.

1. An unpinned session stays on the key it bound after the operator moves the weights to another key.
2. A session whose bound key is disabled moves to a live key, binds it and stays on it against the weights. Two live keys remain, so the session has to notice its key is gone instead of skipping affinity on a one-key pool.
3. A session whose bound key the provider rejects outright (a 401) is served by a live sibling key of the same provider instead of failing, and rebinds to it, so the next request makes a single attempt on the sibling. Before the session's pool carried the rest of the eligible keys, the request ended in the provider's 401. A caller's x-bf-api-key-id pin on the dead key has no pool behind it and still fails with that 401.
4. A session whose bound key is deleted, not disabled, moves to a live key, its trail saying the bound key is no longer eligible, binds it and stays on it against the weights.

Each row creates and deletes its provider through pm.sendRequest and sweeps leftovers older than ten minutes. Row 1 holds the session on B for ten follow-ups, each trail naming the reused key; row 2 re-enables the disabled key and weighs it alone, and the session stays where it moved; row 5 binds a session on three equally weighted keys and reuses the first key for twenty more turns, each trail naming it. Row 6 writes a single-key provider's binding on the first turn and never refreshes it: with a ten-second session TTL, a session that turned at 0s, 4s and 8s has lost its binding at 12.5s while one bound at 8s still holds, and a key added later leaves a default-TTL session on its first key. Row 7 is row 2 with one key left: the bound key B is disabled beside a single key A, so the pool has one key and the session cannot choose, yet it must still drop its binding to B. B is then enabled again and weighted alone, and the session stays on A for three turns while a control request lands on B. Run with FEATURE="session-key-affinity".

item.description: Binds the session to key B (weight 1 beside key A at 0), then disables B, leaving a one-key pool. The next session request must land on A. Then B is enabled again and weighted alone, so ordinary selection always picks it: three more session requests must stay on A, while a control request without the session lands on B. Before the fix, the one-key pool skipped the session and its binding to B survived, so B coming back took the session back.
